processing: Hand-plucked China-type leaf made in the Darjeeling way, mostly as black tea, with oxidation usually lighter in spring than in summer.
harvest_season: Through the Darjeeling flushes; second flush is the picking most tied to muscatel character.
appearance_dry: Small to medium twisted leaf in green and brown, typical of Darjeeling's small-leaved bushes.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in spring to amber in summer, clear.
appearance_wet: Small, narrow leaves in green and copper.
taste_profile: Typical of Darjeeling: floral and brisk in spring, and rounder in summer, with the muscat-like fruit many drinkers associate with these older bushes.

brewing.notes: Usual Darjeeling Western-style start, cooler and shorter for first flush. Taste it without milk.

vintage_note: Sold by estate, flush and harvest year, labelled China, Chinary or Traditional China on lots that separate it from clonal tea. As with other Darjeeling, first flush is for drinking young and second flush keeps a bit longer. Unlabelled Darjeeling may be either type or a mix.
description:
Darjeeling Chinary is not a special tea so much as a plant type: Darjeeling made from China-type bushes rather than selected clones. Despite the name, nothing here says the tea comes from China. The word refers to the variety, sinensis, and the tea is entirely Indian.

Processing is the normal Darjeeling routine, hand-plucked and most often made as black tea. Growers of this type tend to keep it apart from clonal lots when they want the difference to show on the label.

In the cup, expect what Darjeeling is known for: spring florals and brisk dryness, then more body and fruit in summer. Many drinkers tie the classic muscatel note to these bushes, though the insects behind it and the season count for as much. Gopaldhara describes its own Traditional China as having a dual character across the year.

When buying, look for the word China or Chinary together with the estate and flush. Without those details, the word tells you little about quality. It is most interesting tasted beside a clonal lot from the same garden and season.
history: China seed was the first planting material in Darjeeling, arriving in the mid-1800s, which is why China-type bushes are part of the district's older plantings. As new plantings moved to clones, the old type came to need a name of its own, and Chinary and Traditional China became trade terms for tea from it. When that usage began is not well documented.
